h1: Investor Renovation Contractor in Ann Arbor
intro: Nothing in Ann Arbor is cheap, including the mistakes. Acquisition prices are among the highest in Michigan, a dated house still draws owner-occupant competition, and the city layers rental certification, historic district review and energy disclosure on top of ordinary permits. Investors here make money by being precise: knowing what a 1960s Lansdowne ranch really needs, what a converted Kerrytown house can legally hold, and which work must be finished before the August move-in. Genstone Construction gives you that precision before you commit. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the repairs on the specific property and tests them against the resale value or rent your plan assumes. After closing, the project follows a detailed scope and draw schedule, one field manager owns it, and licensed local trades handle the work and the city’s inspections. Draws are released only for completed work, with no money upfront.
housingStock:
Ann Arbor’s housing reads like a timeline of the University of Michigan’s growth. The Old West Side, settled in the mid-nineteenth century by German immigrants, is a dense grid of modest frame houses, gable-fronts and cottages on small lots, many of them in a local historic district. Kerrytown, Lower Town and the Old Fourth Ward, close to downtown and Central Campus, hold some of the oldest houses in the city, including Greek Revival and Italianate homes that were cut into student apartments long ago.

Burns Park, southeast of campus, filled in during the 1910s and 1920s with foursquares, Craftsman houses, Dutch colonials and Tudor revivals on tree-lined streets. Water Hill and Northside mix older cottages with later infill on hilly lots. After the Second World War, the city spread outward: Eberwhite and the west side added bungalows and Cape Cods, while Ann Arbor Hills became home to larger houses, including a number of notable mid-century modern designs by local architects such as Robert Metcalf. Lansdowne, Georgetown and Bryant on the south and southeast sides were built largely in the 1950s through the 1970s with ranches, split-levels and colonials.

For renovation, the older stock brings knob-and-tube wiring, galvanized plumbing, balloon framing, lead paint and stone or brick foundations. The mid-century houses bring their own list: original single-pane or steel windows, flat or low-slope roofs on modern designs, radiant heat in slabs, asbestos in floor tile and duct wrap, and undersized electrical services. Many Ann Arbor homes also have sump pumps that were added when the city disconnected footing drains from the sanitary sewer, and those pumps are now the main defense against a wet basement. Soils add variety: some neighborhoods sit on well-drained sand and gravel, while others have heavy clay that holds water against the walls.

commonIssues.title: Sump pumps from footing drain disconnection
commonIssues.body: For years, Ann Arbor disconnected footing drains from the sanitary sewer in neighborhoods prone to sewer backups, installing sump pumps to handle groundwater instead. Those pumps now protect many basements, but only if they work. A failed pump, a missing check valve or a frozen discharge line can flood a finished basement within hours during a spring storm. We test every sump during a pre-offer review and often recommend battery backup and a high-water alarm.

commonIssues.title: Basement bedrooms and egress
commonIssues.body: Student and multi-tenant houses near campus often use basement rooms as bedrooms, sometimes without proper egress windows, ceiling height or smoke detection. The city’s rental inspection looks closely at sleeping rooms. Adding a code-compliant egress well involves cutting the foundation, installing a window and well, and managing drainage so the new opening does not become a leak. We price that work early because it can determine how many bedrooms a house can legally rent.

commonIssues.title: Mid-century modern repairs
commonIssues.body: Ann Arbor’s mid-century houses are prized by buyers, but they come with particular maintenance needs. Low-slope roofs need careful membrane work and drainage. Steel or single-pane windows lose heat and can condense heavily in winter. Radiant heating in slabs may leak or fail. Original asbestos floor tile is common. Renovating these homes well means respecting their design while upgrading systems, which takes contractors who understand how the houses were built.

commonIssues.title: Historic district limits
commonIssues.body: The Old West Side, Old Fourth Ward, Division Street and several other areas are local historic districts. Exterior work, such as replacing windows, siding, porches, roofing materials and adding dormers or additions, requires approval from the Historic District Commission. Vinyl replacement windows and synthetic siding are often not approved. Investors who plan on fast exterior updates in these neighborhoods should budget for repair of original materials and allow time for the review process.

commonIssues.title: Radon in Washtenaw County homes
commonIssues.body: Washtenaw County is an area where high radon readings turn up often, and buyers here routinely test for it. A poor result can stall a sale or add a mitigation request late in the transaction. For flips and rentals with finished basements, installing a sub-slab mitigation system during the renovation is often easier and cheaper than doing it under pressure after the buyer’s inspection, because the pipe can be routed through a closet or the garage before finishes go in. We include testing and mitigation pricing in the scope when it makes sense.

investorMarket:
Ann Arbor is a high-price, low-inventory city, and that shapes every investor strategy. Classic distressed-property flips are rare because owner-occupants compete for almost everything. The opportunities that do appear tend to be dated houses that need more work than a typical buyer will take on: a Lansdowne or Georgetown ranch with original kitchens and baths, a Burns Park foursquare with tired systems, or an estate sale property that has not been updated in decades. Those can work as flips when the scope is accurate and the finish matches buyers’ expectations, which are high.

Rental investing centers on the university. Houses near Central Campus, Kerrytown, the Old Fourth Ward and around South University and Packard have long been rented to students, often by the room. Demand is steady, leases are signed many months in advance and the academic calendar dictates when work can be done. Graduate students, medical residents and university staff create demand for quieter rentals in Water Hill, Northside and the west side.

BRRRR is harder in Ann Arbor because purchase prices leave little room, but it can work on properties with significant deferred maintenance. Many investors also look to Ypsilanti and surrounding townships, where prices are lower but tenants still commute to Ann Arbor.
permits:
Building, electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits in Ann Arbor are issued by the city’s Building and Rental Services unit, which also administers the rental housing program. Most renovations beyond paint, flooring and like-for-like cabinet replacement require at least one permit, and inspections are required at rough-in and final stages.

Rental properties must have a valid certificate of compliance before they can be occupied, and the city reinspects on a recurring cycle. The certificate lists the maximum number of occupants, which depends on zoning and the house’s features, so bedroom count, egress and parking can directly affect rental income.

The Historic District Commission reviews exterior changes in local historic districts, including the Old West Side and the Old Fourth Ward. Ann Arbor also has a Home Energy Rating Disclosure ordinance that requires most single-family homes to have a home energy score before they are listed for sale, which flippers should plan into their timeline. Properties in the Allen Creek or Huron River floodplains face additional rules. Genstone’s field manager confirms which reviews apply to the property and coordinates permits through the licensed local contractors.
climate: Ann Arbor shares southeast Michigan’s climate: cold, snowy winters, frequent freeze-thaw cycles and warm, humid summers with strong thunderstorms. Winter brings the familiar risk of frozen pipes and ice dams, especially in older homes with little attic insulation. Spring is when basements are tested. Heavy rain on saturated ground pushes groundwater toward foundations, and houses that rely on sump pumps can flood quickly if a pump fails. Low-lying areas along the Huron River and the buried Allen Creek on the west side of downtown are more prone to flooding. Summer humidity drives mold in damp basements. Exterior work such as roofing, masonry and painting is easiest from late spring through early fall, which overlaps with the busy student turnover period near campus.

faqs.q: Can investors still find renovation opportunities in Ann Arbor?
faqs.a: Yes, but they look different from those in lower-priced cities. Most opportunities are dated houses, estate sales and student rentals that need more work than owner-occupants want to tackle. Because prices are high, accuracy matters more than usual. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the specific work the house needs and checks it against realistic resale or rental values, so you can bid with confidence or walk away.

faqs.q: How does the student leasing calendar affect renovations?
faqs.a: Student leases near campus usually turn over in late spring and begin again in late summer. That leaves a short window for major work between move-out and move-in. Larger projects need to be planned months ahead, with permits ready and materials ordered before tenants leave. Our schedules are built backward from move-in day, with the city’s inspection booked ahead of it.

faqs.q: Do I need a home energy score before selling a flip in Ann Arbor?
faqs.a: Under the city’s Home Energy Rating Disclosure ordinance, most single-family homes need a home energy score before they are listed. For flippers, it makes sense to schedule the assessment after insulation, windows and mechanical work are complete, so the score reflects the improvements. We can sequence the work so the house is ready for the assessment when finishes are done.

faqs.q: Do you take on projects in Ypsilanti and the townships around Ann Arbor?
faqs.a: Yes. Our licensed contractors work across Washtenaw County, including Ypsilanti, Pittsfield, Scio, Superior and Ann Arbor townships, Saline and Dexter. Each of those places runs its own building office and treats rental property its own way, so the permit plan follows the parcel. Plenty of investors pair a high-priced Ann Arbor rental with a lower-cost house in Ypsilanti near Eastern Michigan University, and we can keep one specification across both while meeting each city’s rules.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Ann Arbor, MI | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Ann Arbor fix and flip contractor: dated ranches, Burns Park foursquares and estate homes renovated to local buyer expectations, energy score and all.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Ann Arbor
fix-flip.intro: An Ann Arbor flip is judged by buyers who have seen a lot of good houses. Many are university faculty, physicians and professionals who expect thoughtful design, quality materials and documented systems. They will notice a cheap faucet, a crooked tile line or a basement that smells damp. At the same time, purchase prices leave little room for overspending. Genstone Construction helps you plan a flip that meets that standard without blowing the budget. The free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates the cost and compares it with the sales your listing will be measured against. After closing, the project runs from a detailed scope with finish choices, under one field manager, with licensed local trades pulling permits through Building and Rental Services and draws tied to finished work.

sections.h2: The houses that become Ann Arbor flips
sections.body:
In a city where most well-kept homes sell quickly to owner-occupants, flip candidates tend to share a story. They are often estate sales or long-held houses with original kitchens and baths, worn finishes and aging systems. On the south and southeast sides, Lansdowne, Georgetown and Bryant have many 1950s through 1970s ranches, split-levels and colonials in that condition. Buyers like their yards, schools and location but do not want to tackle a full renovation themselves.

Closer to downtown, Burns Park and Eberwhite occasionally offer older foursquares, bungalows and Cape Cods that have not been updated. These carry more risk because of their age, with knob-and-tube wiring, stone or block foundations and lead paint, but they also command strong prices once renovated. Mid-century modern homes in Ann Arbor Hills and similar areas attract a dedicated buyer pool and need specialized care. We look at each property’s condition and the sales it will be compared with before recommending a scope.

Ann Arbor buyers expect a finished product that looks considered rather than flipped. In a 1960s ranch, that often means opening the kitchen to the living area where structure allows, adding a well-designed island, choosing solid cabinets and quartz or similar counters, and updating bathrooms with tile, good lighting and quality fixtures. In older homes, buyers value original woodwork, built-ins and hardwood floors, so restoration often beats replacement.

Systems matter just as much. Buyer inspections here are detailed, and agents commonly order radon tests, sewer scopes and close looks at the electrical panel, furnace and roof. A house with a radon mitigation system, a sewer line in good condition, an updated panel and a dry basement with a working sump and battery backup will move through inspection more smoothly. Energy improvements also count. Because the city requires a home energy score before listing, attic insulation, air sealing, efficient windows and a high-efficiency furnace help the score and the sale.

sections.h2: Timeline and permits for an Ann Arbor flip
sections.body:
Holding costs on an expensive Ann Arbor purchase add up quickly, so the schedule matters. The usual delays come from permit review, hidden conditions and historic district approvals where they apply. Permits from Building and Rental Services are required for most electrical, plumbing, mechanical and structural work, and inspections must be passed at each stage. If the house is in a historic district, exterior changes go to the Historic District Commission, and that review should be scheduled before work begins.

Our detailed scope lists every item with its cost and sequence. The field manager orders the trades so rough-in inspections pass before insulation and drywall, and materials with long lead times, such as windows and custom cabinets, are ordered early. The home energy assessment is scheduled once insulation, windows and mechanicals are complete. When hidden problems appear, like a rotted sill plate or a cracked drain under the slab, the change is priced and photographed in writing before anyone proceeds. That keeps the project moving toward a listing date you can plan around.

faqs.q: Which Ann Arbor neighborhoods are best for flips?
faqs.a: Many flips happen in Lansdowne, Georgetown, Bryant and other areas with 1950s through 1970s housing, because those homes are often dated but structurally straightforward. Older neighborhoods like Burns Park and Eberwhite can also work but carry more risk. Mid-century homes in Ann Arbor Hills have a dedicated buyer pool. In each case, the right scope depends on recent sales nearby, which we review before recommending finishes.

faqs.q: Is radon mitigation worth adding to an Ann Arbor flip?
faqs.a: When the test comes back high, yes. Buyers’ agents in Washtenaw County order radon tests almost by default, and a high number found during the inspection period becomes a negotiation you have little leverage in. A sub-slab system installed while walls are still open can be run neatly through a closet or garage, labeled and tested after installation. Handing the buyer a passing post-mitigation result is a lot simpler than arguing over a credit.

faqs.q: Can original windows be replaced on an Old West Side flip?
faqs.a: Only with Historic District Commission approval, and the commission frequently prefers repair over replacement when original sashes are salvageable. Vinyl units are a hard sell in that review. The practical path is to have the windows assessed early, price both restoration with storm windows and replacement with an approvable product, and submit the application before demolition starts. We prepare the pricing for both options so you can decide which one to take to the commission.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Ann Arbor, MI | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR contractor in Ann Arbor: rehabs that add legal bedrooms, pass rental certification and support the refinance on high-cost Washtenaw County homes.
brrrr.h1: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Ann Arbor
brrrr.intro: BRRRR in Ann Arbor is a different exercise than in Flint or Detroit. The purchase discount is smaller, the rehab budget is larger and the refinance depends on appraisers who compare your house with well-maintained homes nearby. What makes the math work here is usually not a dramatic cosmetic transformation but a change in what the property legally is and can earn: an added egress bedroom, a corrected occupancy limit on the rental certificate, a dry basement that can be used. Genstone Construction scopes rehabs with that in mind. Before you commit, our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review totals the work and holds it up against the rent and appraised value your plan requires. During construction, a field manager runs licensed local contractors from an itemized scope, Building and Rental Services issues permits and inspections, and draws release only for finished work.

sections.h2: Where value is created in an Ann Arbor BRRRR
sections.body:
Appraisers in Ann Arbor evaluate condition, but they also weigh bedrooms, bathrooms and usable square footage. A house that gains a legal bedroom in the basement through a proper egress window, or a second bathroom carved from underused space, can see a larger change in value than one that only receives new finishes. Those same changes often raise rent, especially near campus where rent is driven by the number of bedrooms.

The key word is legal. A basement bedroom without egress, adequate ceiling height and smoke detection will not count with the city’s rental inspection and may not be credited by the appraiser. We look for houses where adding bedrooms or baths is realistic, considering foundation construction, drainage, ceiling heights and zoning. The scope then focuses on those value-creating items, plus the systems and finishes needed to support the appraisal. Our pre-offer review spells out what is possible in the specific house before you commit to the purchase.

In Ann Arbor, the rental certificate of compliance does more than confirm that the house is safe. It sets the maximum number of occupants, which depends on zoning and on the house’s bedrooms, egress, parking and other features. For a BRRRR investor, that number is a key input in both rent and value.

We build the rehab around the certificate. That means correctly sized egress windows in every sleeping room, smoke and carbon monoxide alarms where required, handrails and guardrails, safe electrical systems and adequate heat. Basement bedrooms receive special attention because they are common in student rentals and often fail inspection. Building and Rental Services reinspects rentals periodically, so durable, code-compliant work saves money over the long term. Before you buy, we review the property’s current certificate if one exists, note the occupancy and identify what would be required to change it, so you can see the potential increase in rent and value.

sections.h2: Finishes and systems that last near campus
sections.body:
Rentals near campus see hard use. Tenants turn over frequently, and furniture moves in and out every year. Finishes need to handle that without looking cheap, because appraisers and future tenants in Ann Arbor still expect a good-looking house.

We usually recommend waterproof plank flooring in most areas, durable quartz or solid-surface counters, sturdy cabinets with soft-close hardware, washable paint and commercial-grade door hardware. Bathrooms benefit from tile surrounds and exhaust fans on timers to control moisture from several showers a morning. On the systems side, a high-efficiency furnace, an electrical service sized for more occupants and their devices, a reliable water heater and a sump pump with battery backup are worth the investment. Attic insulation and air sealing help with tenant comfort and energy costs, and they support a better home energy score if you eventually sell. Every line in the scope should either raise the appraisal, protect the occupancy limit or cut the cost of the next August turnover.

faqs.q: Can I add a basement bedroom in an Ann Arbor rental?
faqs.a: Often, if the basement has enough ceiling height, a suitable wall for an egress window and good drainage. Adding egress involves cutting the foundation, installing a window and well and managing water. The bedroom must also meet the city’s rental inspection requirements. We evaluate the basement before you buy so you know whether a legal bedroom is realistic and what it would cost.

faqs.q: Where do I find the occupancy limit for an Ann Arbor rental?
faqs.a: On the rental certificate of compliance, if the house already has one. That number reflects zoning plus features such as the count of legal bedrooms, egress and parking, and it can be one of the most valuable facts about the property. Before you buy, we read the existing certificate, walk the house against it and tell you which changes, if any, could support a different limit and roughly what they would cost to build.

faqs.q: Does BRRRR actually pencil out at Ann Arbor prices?
faqs.a: Sometimes, and rarely by accident. The deals that work tend to involve a house with heavy deferred maintenance that scared off owner-occupants, or one where a legal bedroom or second bath can be added. Cosmetic-only rehabs seldom create enough gap between cost and value. Our pre-offer review tests the specific property, and many investors run their BRRRR projects in Ypsilanti or the townships while holding Ann Arbor houses for long-term rent.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Ann Arbor, MI | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Ann Arbor rental renovation: student and staff rentals updated around the lease calendar, built to the city's rental certificate and periodic reinspection.
rental-renovation.h1: Rental Property Renovation in Ann Arbor
rental-renovation.intro: Owning rentals in Ann Arbor means working on a schedule set by the University of Michigan. Leases near campus turn over in a short window each year, and a house that is not ready on move-in day creates problems for a whole group of tenants. Rentals away from campus serve graduate students, medical residents, hospital staff and young professionals who expect a quiet, well-kept home. Genstone Construction renovates and turns rental houses across Ann Arbor with both groups in mind. We help owners settle on a portfolio specification, then price each house separately under one field manager, using licensed trades who know what Ann Arbor’s rental inspectors check. Genstone Field Services can handle inspections, occupied maintenance, turns and code compliance throughout the year, so properties stay certified and ready for the next lease.

sections.h2: Working the Ann Arbor lease calendar
sections.body:
Near Central Campus, Kerrytown, the Old Fourth Ward and the South University area, leases typically run from late summer to the following spring. That leaves a compressed window for turnover and renovation each year, when many owners need contractors at once. Planning ahead is the only way to get major work done during that period.

We start planning months before move-out. That means walking each property during the school year, with notice to tenants, to identify needed repairs, preparing scopes and estimates, applying for permits and ordering materials with long lead times. When tenants move out, crews can begin immediately. Larger projects, such as kitchen remodels, bathroom additions or egress windows, are scheduled first, while smaller turns follow. New tenants cannot move in until the house passes the city’s inspection, so the turnover plan reserves the last stretch of summer for that visit and any fixes. For rentals off campus, leases are more varied, and turns can be scheduled throughout the year.

Ann Arbor requires a rental certificate of compliance for rental properties and reinspects on a recurring cycle. Inspectors focus on life safety items such as smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, egress from sleeping rooms, handrails, electrical safety, heating and general maintenance. In older houses near campus, basement bedrooms, attic rooms and exterior stairs are frequent trouble spots, and a single failed bedroom can affect how many tenants the house may hold.

We build certificate requirements into every renovation and turn. Before each inspection, a crew member walks the house against the inspector’s list: alarm locations and dates, egress window operation, stair rails, outlet covers and panel labeling, heat and plumbing. Peeling paint in pre-1978 houses is addressed with lead-safe practices. If an inspector cites something, we come back to fix it and line up the follow-up visit with Building and Rental Services. Keeping a record of what was installed and repaired in each property also helps with future inspections and with answering tenant questions, and for owners with many properties it makes certificates across the portfolio far easier to track.

sections.h2: A rental standard for Ann Arbor houses
sections.body:
An Ann Arbor rental standard has to account for two kinds of tenants and a wide range of housing, from nineteenth-century houses near Kerrytown to 1970s colonials on the south side. For student houses, the standard emphasizes durability: waterproof plank flooring, washable paint, sturdy cabinets and counters, commercial-grade door hardware and bathroom exhaust fans that actually move air. For staff and graduate tenants, the standard can include slightly better finishes and more attention to quiet and comfort, such as insulation and solid doors.

Mechanically, the standard should include high-efficiency furnaces, updated electrical panels with enough capacity for modern use, reliable water heaters and sump pumps with battery backup and alarms where basements rely on them. Attic insulation and air sealing reduce heating bills, which tenants notice in February. Using one product list across a Burns Park duplex, a Water Hill cottage and a Bryant colonial means a single box of spare cartridges, filters and hinges covers the whole portfolio, and repair calls get resolved on the first trip.

faqs.q: When should I schedule renovation work on a student rental?
faqs.a: Plan months ahead and schedule the work for the period between move-out and move-in. Walk the property during the school year, prepare the scope, apply for permits and order materials before tenants leave. Larger projects should be scheduled first in the turnover window. We help owners plan these timelines so units are ready for the city’s inspection and for the next tenants.

faqs.q: Can maintenance be handled while students are living in the house?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Field Services does repairs and inspections in occupied homes through the school year. Your property manager arranges entry and the tenants get notice, which matters in a house with five or six schedules. Water and heat interruptions are kept short, and in older houses any cutting into painted trim or plaster is contained and cleaned up. Mid-year visits are also a good time to test sump pumps and check rails before the reinspection comes due.

faqs.q: Will you work on my rentals in Ypsilanti as well?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Ann Arbor landlords also own near Eastern Michigan University, where purchase prices are lower and student demand is steady. Ypsilanti runs its own building department and rental inspection program, and the housing tends to be older frame stock with its own repair patterns. We keep a single finish specification across both cities where it makes sense and adjust the permit and inspection plan for each address.

multifamily-renovation.title: Small Multifamily Renovation in Ann Arbor, MI | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Ann Arbor 2–4 unit renovation: converted houses near campus, basement egress, fire separation, occupancy limits and work timed to the student lease cycle.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and Small Multifamily Renovation in Ann Arbor
multifamily-renovation.intro: Small multifamily in Ann Arbor usually means a house that the university turned into apartments. Around Central Campus, Kerrytown, the Old Fourth Ward and the blocks off South University and Packard, large nineteenth and early twentieth century homes were split into two, three or four units, often with additional bedrooms tucked into attics and basements. There are also purpose-built duplexes and small apartment buildings scattered across older neighborhoods. These buildings can produce strong rent, but they are heavily regulated and often carry decades of improvised alterations. Our approach to these Ann Arbor buildings starts from those realities. We plan shared systems, egress and fire separation first, write a detailed scope, assign one field manager and coordinate licensed local trades who pull permits through Building and Rental Services.

sections.h2: Inside a converted house near campus
sections.body:
Converted houses near campus typically have a unit on each floor, with additional sleeping rooms in the attic or basement. Over many decades, owners added kitchens, bathrooms, partitions and exterior stairs to fit more tenants. Some changes were permitted, while others were not. The result can be a building with electrical services split in unusual ways, plumbing stacks serving multiple units, bedrooms without proper egress and fire separation that has been compromised by openings and chases.

When you buy one of these buildings, the shared and hidden issues usually determine the budget. We look at the electrical service, panels and circuits; plumbing stacks and drains; fire separation between units; exterior stairs and porches; roofs; and foundations. Basement and attic bedrooms get special attention because the city’s rental inspection scrutinizes them. In historic districts like the Old Fourth Ward, exterior changes such as new stairs or windows require Historic District Commission review, which affects both the design and the schedule.

In Ann Arbor, the number of people a building can legally house depends on zoning and on the rental certificate, which considers bedrooms, egress and other features. Improving egress and fire safety can protect the building’s occupancy, and in some cases support an increase, which directly affects income. Losing a bedroom at reinspection does the opposite.

Typical work includes adding egress windows to basement bedrooms, upgrading attic rooms with proper exits, installing fire-rated drywall and self-closing doors between units, sealing penetrations around pipes and ducts and installing interconnected smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. Exterior stairs may need rebuilding to meet current standards, which in a historic district also means a design the commission will accept. Electrical services often need upgrading to handle multiple units with modern appliances, and separating meters lets tenants pay their own utility bills. Each element carries its own permit and inspection with Building and Rental Services. We lay out a plan for the entire building so you can see how each change affects cost, compliance and occupancy before you commit.

sections.h2: Timing renovations to the lease cycle
sections.body:
Multi-unit buildings near campus usually have every lease starting and ending on the same dates, which compresses renovation into a few summer weeks. Large projects, such as fire separation, egress windows and electrical service upgrades, need to be planned during the school year, with drawings, permits and materials ready before the last tenant hands back keys.

When only some units are empty over the summer, building-wide work is grouped into brief shutdowns that tenants hear about in advance, and the occupied apartments keep their access, heat and water. Lead-safe practices are essential in older buildings because dust can travel between units through stairwells and shared basements. If a project is too large for one turnover period, we split it over two summers, putting egress and fire separation in year one and finishing kitchens and baths in year two. Every unit has to pass the city’s inspection before move-in, so the schedule leaves room for that visit and any corrections. Planned this way, the building keeps earning while it improves.

faqs.q: Could my Ann Arbor building legally house more tenants after a renovation?
faqs.a: It might, but nothing is automatic. The limit printed on the rental certificate reflects zoning along with bedrooms, egress, parking and other features, and some upgrades move that number while others do not. We start with the certificate and the floor plans, identify which changes could matter, and give you a cost for each so you can decide whether the added rent justifies the work before applying for anything.

faqs.q: How do historic district rules affect a multi-unit near campus?
faqs.a: If the building sits in a local district such as the Old Fourth Ward or Old West Side, the Historic District Commission reviews exterior changes, which on a rental often means new exit stairs, egress windows, porches and siding. Interior work is generally outside that review. We design exterior safety improvements so they are compatible with the house and build the commission’s calendar into the schedule, because a stair that cannot be approved in time can hold up a whole lease cycle.

faqs.q: Can a big renovation be split over more than one summer?
faqs.a: Yes, and for many older buildings near campus it is the only realistic way. We rank the work by risk and requirement, putting egress, fire separation, electrical service and roof work in the first phase and kitchens, baths and cosmetic upgrades in the next. Each phase gets its own scope, price and permit set, and the plan is written so the building stays compliant with its rental certificate at every stage in between.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Ann Arbor, MI | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor in Ann Arbor: bids for dated ranches, older homes and owner-occupied duplexes, with consultant and draw coordination.
fha-203k.h1: FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor in Ann Arbor
fha-203k.intro: In a city where move-in-ready houses sell quickly and at high prices, the FHA 203(k) loan gives Ann Arbor buyers a way into homes that others pass over. A buyer can purchase a dated south side ranch, a Burns Park house that needs systems work or an owner-occupied duplex near campus and roll the cost of fixing it into that same loan. As a certified FHA 203(k) contractor, Genstone prepares detailed bids, coordinate with HUD consultants, schedule draw inspections and keep permit records from Building and Rental Services. One field manager carries the job, licensed Washtenaw County trades build it, and money moves on the loan’s draw schedule. Buyers and agents can see progress and documentation at every stage.

sections.h2: Ann Arbor houses that fit the program
sections.body:
The 203(k) is a good fit for Ann Arbor houses that are structurally sound but dated. Ranches, split-levels and colonials in Lansdowne, Georgetown, Bryant and similar neighborhoods often need kitchen and bath updates, new windows, roof replacement, furnace and water heater replacement and electrical upgrades. Those projects usually fit the Limited 203(k).

Older homes in Burns Park, Eberwhite, Water Hill and the Old West Side can also work, but the scope can grow quickly with foundation repairs, rewiring, plumbing and lead paint. Historic district rules affect exterior work on the Old West Side and similar areas. Owner-occupied duplexes and small multi-units near campus can qualify if the buyer lives in one unit, and the rental income can help the buyer qualify. Those buildings often need fire separation and egress work. FHA loan limits also apply, and in Ann Arbor’s price range, they can constrain the total project. We help buyers and lenders see whether the numbers work before the buyer pays for appraisals and consultants.

Ann Arbor buyers and loan officers should decide between the two versions early, and the basement usually settles it. The Limited 203(k) handles non-structural work and caps the repair budget at $75,000. A dated Lansdowne or Bryant house that needs a kitchen and bath, new windows, a roof without sheathing replacement, a furnace and water heater, a panel upgrade, flooring and paint fits comfortably. Radon mitigation and sump pump replacement can be included as well.

The Standard 203(k) begins at a $5,000 minimum, requires a HUD-approved consultant and is the route for structural work. In Ann Arbor that most often means cutting a foundation wall for an egress window, repairing a cracked or bowing basement wall, taking out a bearing wall to open a mid-century kitchen, building an addition or reconfiguring a small multi-unit near campus. Program inspection rules tighten once repairs pass the $15,000 threshold. Our scope labels every structural item, so the lender can select the correct program before the appraisal is ordered rather than after.

Ann Arbor 203(k) files require clear documentation. Lenders need a contractor bid listing each repair with its cost and materials, and Standard loans require the bid to match the consultant’s work write-up. Our bids are written in that format and carry permit costs from Building and Rental Services and, where applicable, the cost of historic district review.

Once the buyer closes, the renovation money is parked with the lender and paid out stage by stage. Before each draw, the consultant or lender inspects the work. Our field manager schedules those inspections, provides photos and documentation, confirms the related city inspections have passed and collects lien waivers from contractors. When opening a wall turns up something new, like rot at a bathroom subfloor, the lender and consultant see photos and a price before that work is added. Buyers receive regular updates. For owner-occupied duplexes, we also coordinate with the rental inspection so units are ready to be leased when the work is complete.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) loan be used on an owner-occupied duplex in Ann Arbor?
faqs.a: Yes. FHA allows the renovation loan on buildings with up to four units, provided the buyer makes one of them their home, and projected rent from the other units may help the buyer qualify. Near campus, the older duplexes and converted houses that fit this description often need fire separation, egress and electrical service work before the rental side can pass the city’s inspection, so we price those shared items first and the unit interiors second.

faqs.q: Will FHA loan limits cap a 203(k) project in Ann Arbor?
faqs.a: They can. FHA sets a maximum loan amount by county, and in Ann Arbor’s price range the purchase plus renovation may run close to the Washtenaw County figure. Your loan officer will have the current number. If the combined total runs too high, we can phase lower-priority items out of the scope and keep the work that matters most to safety, systems and value, so the buyer still ends up with a sound house.

faqs.q: Are radon mitigation and a new sump pump eligible 203(k) repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. Both are legitimate repairs under the program and often belong in an Ann Arbor scope, given how common high radon readings are in Washtenaw County and how many basements depend on a sump installed under the footing drain disconnection program. We write each as a separate line with the system type and discharge location so the consultant and appraiser can see exactly what is being installed and why.

reo-renovation.title: REO Property Renovation in Ann Arbor, MI | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: Ann Arbor REO and bank-owned renovation for servicers, banks and GSEs: sump failures, freeze damage and rental-code issues repaired with full records.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Ann Arbor
reo-renovation.intro: REO inventory in Ann Arbor is small, and well-presented properties sell quickly in this market. That makes the period between takeover and listing especially valuable. A bank-owned house here might be a dated ranch that needs cleaning and paint, or a converted rental near campus with code issues and a basement flooded by a failed sump pump. Genstone Construction prepares Ann Arbor REO homes for sale on behalf of servicers, lenders, REITs, funds and the Government-Sponsored Enterprises, where Genstone holds preferred-contractor status, and we adapt to each client’s bid layout, photo rules and approval thresholds. Our estimators write line-item bids, a field manager oversees each property and licensed local trades work under city permits. Genstone Field Services can keep the house secured, winterized, inspected and maintained from the day of takeover to the day it lists.

sections.h2: Vacancy damage in Ann Arbor homes
sections.body:
The most damaging problem in vacant Ann Arbor houses is often water from below. Many homes rely on sump pumps installed under the city’s footing drain disconnection program. When a house is vacant, the power may be shut off, a pump may fail or a discharge line may freeze. During a spring storm, groundwater can fill the basement, soaking finished walls, flooring, furnaces and water heaters. Mold follows quickly.

Winter brings the other familiar risk. If heat is off, pipes freeze and split, and a burst pipe can flood multiple floors. Ice dams on poorly insulated roofs push water into ceilings and walls. Vacant houses may also suffer from deferred maintenance, pest intrusion and occasional vandalism. Our estimators document each condition with photos, test the sump pump and look for signs of past flooding, so the bid reflects the property’s actual condition. That gives the asset manager a clear basis for approving repairs.

sections.h2: Rental code, historic rules and marketability
sections.body:
Many Ann Arbor REO properties were rentals, and they may carry open issues with the city’s rental certificate, such as missing smoke alarms, basement bedrooms without egress or unpermitted alterations. An investor buyer will need to bring the property into compliance, and those issues reduce the price they are willing to pay. Correcting them before sale can broaden the buyer pool.

Owner-occupant buyers using FHA or conventional financing need a house with working systems, a sound roof, safe electrical service and no peeling paint on pre-1978 homes. Radon is also a frequent concern in Washtenaw County, and mitigation may make the property easier to sell. Properties in historic districts need Historic District Commission approval for exterior changes, which affects the scope and schedule. We review the property’s permit and rental history where available and recommend a scope that fits the expected buyer. Permits are pulled through Building and Rental Services, and records are kept in the project file.

sections.h2: Records an asset manager can approve from
sections.body:
On a high-value Ann Arbor property, an asset manager needs to approve repairs quickly and still be able to justify them months later. Our bids put each repair on its own line, separate labor from materials, include dumpster and disposal costs from the start and attach photographs to every line so the reviewer can see the condition behind the cost.

While work is underway, the field manager reports against those approved lines. Anything new, such as mold behind finished basement drywall after a sump failure or a cracked cast-iron drain under the slab, comes in as a change order with photos and a short explanation before the extra work proceeds. Lien waivers are collected from each trade at payment, and the project file is organized for audit. Because Genstone also operates Field Services, snow removal, lawn care, re-securing, winterization and periodic inspections run on the same calendar as construction. In a market where buyers are waiting, that coordination shortens the time from takeover to listing.

faqs.q: What should be checked first on an Ann Arbor REO?
faqs.a: The sump pump and the heat. Many Ann Arbor basements depend on sump pumps, and a vacant house without power or with a failed pump can flood quickly. In winter, the plumbing must be protected from freezing. Genstone Field Services can test the pump, restore or confirm power, winterize the plumbing and secure the property while the asset manager reviews the scope.

faqs.q: Which REO clients do you serve in Washtenaw County?
faqs.a: Our Ann Arbor REO work comes from loan servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and the GSEs, which list Genstone as a preferred contractor. We follow each client’s bid template and photo requirements. On Ann Arbor files we add notes that matter locally, such as the status of any rental certificate, unpermitted basement bedrooms, historic district designation and whether the house depends on a sump pump, so the asset manager understands what a buyer will see.

faqs.q: Should an Ann Arbor REO be repaired before listing?
faqs.a: Usually, at least to the point where owner-occupants can finance the house. Ann Arbor has strong buyer demand, and a property that qualifies for FHA or conventional financing will reach a larger pool. Addressing rental code issues can also help if investors are likely buyers. We price different levels of repair so the asset manager can compare them with expected sale prices.
